Output? A stream with filter that prints, and no terminal operation.
Output? A pipeline with filter, map and limit(1) over 1, 2, 3, 4, keeping evens and multiplying by 10.

filter 1
filter 2
map 2
[20]
Verified. Elements flow one at a time through the whole chain. 1 fails the filter and never reaches map. 2 passes and goes through map and limit, and limit then requests cancellation, so 3 and 4 are never pulled. People who assume each step runs over the whole list get this wrong.
Output? Stream.of(3,1,2).peek(before).sorted().peek(after).findFirst()

before 3
before 1
before 2
after 1
Verified. sorted is a barrier that must see every element, so all three pass the first peek. After sorting it pushes downstream, and findFirst cancels after the first, so only 1 reaches the second peek.
Output? List.of(1,2,3).stream().peek(System.out::println).count(). And with a filter added?

The first prints just the count, 3 (verified). Since Java 9, count() can compute the size directly from a SIZED source, and it skips the pipeline when nothing can change the count. map in that position was skipped as well.
With .filter(x -> true) the size isn't known in advance, so the pipeline runs and the output is 1, 2, 3, then the count 3.
Can you reuse a stream? What exactly happens?

No. The second terminal operation throws java.lang.IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed (verified). The same error appears if you call an intermediate operation twice on the same stage, because each stage can only be linked once. To run a pipeline twice, create it again: Supplier<Stream<String>> s = () -> list.stream().filter(...); s.get().count(); s.get().toList();
How does a lambda compile? How is it different from an anonymous class?

javac moves the body into a private synthetic method such as lambda$main$0, with captured variables as leading parameters. At the use site it emits invokedynamic. On the first run, the JVM's bootstrap method LambdaMetafactory spins a hidden class that implements the interface and links the call site. No .class file exists for the lambda.
An anonymous class is an ordinary class with its own class file, makes a new object on every evaluation, always captures the enclosing instance in an instance context, and has its own this. Reasons for invokedynamic: smaller class files, lazy linkage, no outer reference unless needed, and freedom for the JVM to change the strategy later.
Output? this in a lambda vs an anonymous class.

outer / F
inner / F$1
For the code in the Lambda Syntax section, verified. In the lambda, this is the enclosing F instance. In the anonymous class, it's the anonymous object, whose own name field shadows the outer one. Anonymous classes create a new scope, and lambdas don't.
Why must captured variables be effectively final? Does that make lambdas thread-safe?

A lambda can outlive the stack frame it was created in, and may run on another thread. So it gets a copy of the value. If the original could change, the copy would go stale without warning, and the language would seem to allow shared mutable locals across threads. Forbidding reassignment keeps the copy always correct.
It doesn't make lambdas thread-safe. Only the variable is fixed. The object it refers to can still be mutated, and fields can be changed too. list.forEach(x -> holder.count++) compiles and races in parallel.
Why doesn't this compile? for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) run(() -> print(i));

i is reassigned by i++, so it's not effectively final, and javac reports local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final. Copy it inside the loop: int j = i; run(() -> print(j));. Each iteration gets a new j: three suppliers built that way returned [0, 1, 2] when run. An enhanced for variable needs no copy, since each iteration declares a new one.
Is Comparator a functional interface, given it has two abstract methods listed?

Yes. It declares compare and equals, but equals matches a public method of Object, which every implementation inherits, so it doesn't count. compare is the only real abstract method. All the others are default or static.
Why do primitive functional interfaces exist? What's the difference between Function<T,T> and UnaryOperator<T>?

Generic interfaces work on objects, so Function<Integer, Integer> boxes every value, adding allocation and indirection. IntUnaryOperator works on raw ints. It matters in hot loops and numeric streams.
UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T, T>. It behaves identically, only stating that input and output types match. List.replaceAll takes it, so a plain Function variable won't compile there. BinaryOperator<T> relates to BiFunction<T, T, T> in the same way.
Output? dbl.andThen(inc).apply(5) and dbl.compose(inc).apply(5), where dbl doubles and inc adds 1.
11 and 12 (verified). andThen runs dbl first: 5 × 2 + 1. compose runs inc first: (5 + 1) × 2.
Explain the four kinds of method reference. What does String::length become?

Static (Math::abs), bound to an instance (System.out::println), unbound (String::length) and constructor (ArrayList::new). String::length is unbound: the function's first argument becomes the receiver, so it's s -> s.length(), which fits Function<String, Integer>. The compiler picks the kind from the target type.
The difference shows with a bound receiver that is null: str::length throws at creation, while () -> str.length() throws only when called (verified).
A class inherits the same default method from two interfaces. What happens?

A compile error, unless the class overrides it. Inside the override, it can call Walker.super.move(). The compiler resolves in this order: a class or superclass method wins, then the most specific sub-interface, and otherwise you must override. In the section's example, new Dog().move() gave class, new Cat().move() gave run, and Duck gave walk+swim (all verified).
Stateless vs stateful operations: why does it matter?

Stateless operations work on each element independently, so they run in constant memory, parallelize trivially, and pass elements straight through. Stateful ones (sorted, distinct, limit, skip) keep information across elements. sorted and distinct can use memory in proportion to the input, sorted can't work on an infinite stream, and in ordered parallel streams they need synchronization or buffering. So cheap filters should come before them: filter then sorted, not the other way round.
How does a stream avoid doing unnecessary work? Name the mechanisms.

- Laziness: nothing runs before the terminal operation.
- Loop fusion: all stages run in a single pass through sinks, not one pass per operation.
- Short-circuiting: sinks report cancellationRequested, and the source stops.
- Flags: known characteristics skip work. For instance, sorted() on an already-sorted stream, distinct() on a distinct stream, and count() on a sized stream.
- Pre-sizing: SIZED lets toArray allocate the exact length.
Stream vs Collection vs Iterator?

| Collection | Iterator | Stream
Holds data | Yes | No | No
Iteration | External | External, you pull | Internal, library pushes
Reusable | Yes | No | No
Evaluation | Eager | On demand | Lazy
Infinite | No | Possible | Possible
Parallel | Do it yourself | Do it yourself | Built in
Modifies source | Yes | remove | No
Stream.toList() vs collect(Collectors.toList())?

toList() (Java 16) gives an unmodifiable list and allows nulls. collect(toList()) gives a list with no documented mutability, which is an ArrayList in practice. toUnmodifiableList() is unmodifiable and rejects nulls.
All verified: Stream.of(1).toList().add(2) threw UnsupportedOperationException. Stream.of("a", null).toList() printed [a, null]. collect(toUnmodifiableList()) on the same input threw NullPointerException.
Output? Stream.of("a","a").collect(toMap(x -> x, x -> 1))

Throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key a (attempted merging values 1 and 1) (verified). With duplicates possible, give a merge function: toMap(k, v, Integer::sum) or (a, b) -> a. A null value gives NullPointerException, even though the map is a HashMap, because it uses merge.
groupingBy vs partitioningBy? What does partitioningBy return with no matches?

groupingBy uses any classifier and only includes keys that occur. partitioningBy takes a predicate and always returns both true and false, in a specialized map. With no matches it gave {false=[...all...], true=[]} (verified). Prefer it for two-way splits, since you can read both keys with no null check.
What's a downstream collector? Give examples.

The collector that groupingBy or partitioningBy applies to each group, in place of toList(). They compose:
groupingBy(Emp::dept, counting())                       // count per dept
groupingBy(Emp::dept, averagingDouble(Emp::salary))     // average per dept
groupingBy(Emp::dept, mapping(Emp::name, toSet()))      // names per dept
groupingBy(Emp::dept, maxBy(comparingDouble(Emp::salary)))           // Optional per dept
groupingBy(Emp::dept, collectingAndThen(counting(), Long::intValue)) // Integer count
groupingBy(Emp::dept, groupingBy(Emp::age))             // two levels
reduce vs collect: which one and why?

reduce combines values into a new immutable value at each step: sum, max, string of a few parts. It treats values as immutable. collect accumulates into a mutable container: a list, map or StringBuilder. Each parallel chunk gets its own container, and they merge at the end.
Using reduce to build a list either copies repeatedly, which is O(n²), or mutates a shared identity, which is wrong in parallel. Rule: if the result is a container, use collect.
Output? List.of(1,2,3).parallelStream().reduce(10, Integer::sum)

It printed 36, while the sequential version gave 16. 10 isn't an identity for addition, so each of the three chunks added it: 11 + 12 + 13. The exact number depends on how the source splits, so this is not a dependable result. Correct is reduce(0, Integer::sum) + 10. Similarly, a non-associative function such as subtraction gave 0 in parallel and -36 in sequence.
Three-argument reduce: what is the combiner for?

When the result type differs from the element type, the accumulator can't merge two partial results. In reduce(0, (sum, word) -> sum + word.length(), Integer::sum), the accumulator takes (Integer, String) and the combiner takes (Integer, Integer). In a parallel run, the combiner merges chunk results. In a sequential run it's not called in the current implementation, which is why broken combiners go unnoticed until someone adds parallel(). Often mapToInt(String::length).sum() is the better form.
Output? Stream.of(new int[]{1,2,3}).count() and Arrays.asList(new int[]{1,2,3}).size()
Both are 1 (verified). Generic T can't be a primitive, so int[] is taken as one object, not as varargs. Arrays.stream(int[]) gives an IntStream of 3, and Stream.of(new Integer[]{1,2,3}) gives 3.
Output? "abc".chars().forEach(System.out::print)

979899 (verified). chars() returns an IntStream of UTF-16 code units, so it prints the numbers. Use .mapToObj(c -> (char) c) to get abc. For text beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane, use codePoints().
Output? allMatch, noneMatch and anyMatch on an empty stream.

true, true, false (verified, even with predicates that always return false for allMatch). This is vacuous truth: "all elements match" can't be disproved with no elements. Be careful in validation: items.stream().allMatch(Item::isValid) is true for an empty order.
findFirst vs findAny? What if the found element is null?

findFirst respects encounter order. findAny may return any element, which lets a parallel stream stop as soon as any chunk finds one. Sequentially, it usually gives the first, but don't rely on that.
Both return Optional, which can't hold null, so a matched null throws NullPointerException (verified on a stream filtered to its null element).
What's wrong with this? list.stream().filter(...).forEach(result::add);

It's a side effect in place of a result. It works by luck sequentially. With parallel() on an ArrayList it loses elements or throws: a test of 100,000 elements kept 26,072, and the number varies per run. It also obscures the intent. Replace it with List<T> result = list.stream().filter(...).toList();. Reserve forEach for real output, such as logging or sending.
What is the point of peek? Can it be used to modify elements?

Its documented purpose is to support debugging. It doesn't guarantee it'll run: count() may skip it, and short-circuiting skips elements. Mutating elements in peek, such as peek(e -> e.setActive(true)), is a hidden side effect that can silently disappear. Use map to return a new value, or a plain loop to mutate.
Output? Add to an ArrayList inside its own stream's forEach. And what about adding after stream() but before the terminal?
Does this stream run forever? Stream.iterate(0, i -> i + 1).sorted().limit(5). And with limit before sorted?

With sorted first, a terminal operation never finishes, and memory grows until OutOfMemoryError, because sorted must buffer an infinite input. With limit(5).sorted(), it finishes at once. Order of operations changes results, not just speed. A related trap: Stream.generate(() -> 1).distinct().limit(2) never ends, because only one distinct value ever appears, so distinct keeps pulling while it waits for a second.
Why does this fail to compile? list.sort(Comparator.comparing(s -> s.length()).reversed())

cannot find symbol: method length(), checked with javac. Inference flows from the target type, but a chained method call has none: comparing is the receiver of .reversed(), so T defaults to Object. Fixes: use a method reference (Comparator.comparing(String::length).reversed(), which ran fine), give the lambda a type ((String s) -> s.length()), or add a type witness (Comparator.<String, Integer>comparing(...)).
When should you use a parallel stream? Why might it be slower?

Use it for large or expensive CPU-bound work, on a well-splitting source, with stateless functions, when spare cores exist, and only after measuring. It can be slower because of split and merge overhead, ordering constraints, boxing, poor sources such as LinkedList, and merging maps in groupingBy. Inside a server, it shares the JVM-wide common pool, so one heavy request affects all others. Blocking I/O in it is the worst case.
Does parallelStream preserve order?

It depends on the operation. If the source is ordered, toList(), collect(toList()), map, limit, reduce and forEachOrdered all respect encounter order in the result. IntStream.range(0, 1000).parallel().boxed().toList() had 999 at index 999, and .limit(3) gave [0, 1, 2]. forEach does not keep order, and its output varies. Execution order is always arbitrary, so side effects in map can run out of order, even when the result is ordered.

What are Gatherers? How do they differ from Collectors?

Custom intermediate operations, added by JEP 485, final in Java 24. Stream.gather(gatherer) lets you transform elements many-to-many with private state, and stop early. Built-ins in Gatherers: fold, scan, windowFixed, windowSliding and mapConcurrent.
A collector ends a stream with one result. A gatherer sits in the middle, emits a stream, can be chained and works with infinite input. So a sliding window or running total, which were awkward before, is one line.
When would you use mapMulti instead of flatMap?

When each element yields few results, so creating a stream per element is wasteful, or when the logic is easier to write imperatively, such as a recursive walk or a type check. flatMap is usually more readable for a plain "each has a collection" case. mapMulti (Java 16) needs a type witness if the compiler can't infer it: .<Integer>mapMulti(...).
Output? Optional.of("x").orElse(say("a")) vs orElseGet(() -> say("b"))

The first prints evaluated a and returns x; the second prints nothing and returns x (verified). orElse's argument is evaluated before the call. If the fallback queries a database or saves a record, it happens every time. Use orElseGet for anything not already computed.
Optional.of vs ofNullable? map vs flatMap on Optional?

Optional.of(null) throws NullPointerException at once, so use it when null would be a bug. ofNullable(null) gives empty.
map wraps the function's result, and a null result becomes empty. flatMap expects the function to return an Optional and doesn't wrap again. With User.getAddress() returning Optional<Address>, map gives Optional<Optional<Address>>, and flatMap gives Optional<Address>.
Should you use Optional as a field or method parameter?

Generally no. As a field, it isn't Serializable, so it breaks Java serialization and needs configuration in some frameworks, and it adds an object per instance. As a parameter, it forces callers to wrap values, and they can still pass null, so you now have three states. Keep nullable fields private and expose Optional from the getter, and use overloads for optional parameters. Also never return Optional<List>: return an empty list.
Does Optional remove the need for null checks? What's its cost?

No. It documents one return value's contract, and a caller can still call get() blindly, or a method can wrongly return null. It's one more object, usually short-lived, so it matters only on very hot paths. There, a null check or sentinel is fine. The value is API clarity, not performance or safety by force.

How do you turn a List<Optional<T>> into a List<T> of the present values?

Since Java 9, Optional.stream() returns a stream of zero or one elements, so flatMap drops the empty ones:
List<User> found = ids.stream()
        .map(repo::findById)          // Stream<Optional<User>>
        .flatMap(Optional::stream)    // only the present values
        .toList();
Before Java 9, you had to write .filter(Optional::isPresent).map(Optional::get). mapMulti also works, but Optional::stream is the idiomatic form.
How do you create a stream from an Iterable or an Iterator?

Iterable has no stream() method (only Collection does), so go through a Spliterator:
Stream<T> s1 = StreamSupport.stream(iterable.spliterator(), false);   // false = sequential
Stream<T> s2 = StreamSupport.stream(
        Spliterators.spliteratorUnknownSize(iterator, Spliterator.ORDERED), false);
Spring Data's findAll() on CrudRepository returns Iterable, which is a common place to need this. ListCrudRepository (Spring Data 3) returns a List instead. An iterator-based spliterator has an unknown size, so it parallelizes poorly.
How do you debug a stream pipeline that gives the wrong result?

- Use the IDE's stream debugger (IntelliJ "Trace Current Stream Chain"), which shows each element at every stage.
- Add temporary peek(e -> log.debug("after filter: {}", e)) calls between stages, and remember that laziness and short-circuiting mean some elements never reach later stages.
- Replace complex lambdas with named methods (.filter(this::isEligible)), so they can be unit-tested and appear clearly in stack traces.
- Split a long chain into named intermediate variables, or collect to a list at a midpoint while investigating.
Explain currying with an example. Is it common in Java?

Currying turns f(a, b) into a -> (b -> result), for example Function<Integer, Function<Integer, Integer>> add = a -> b -> a + b; add.apply(2).apply(3), which gives 5. Its practical value is partial application: building specialized functions from general ones (discount.apply(0.1) gives a "10% off" function). Full currying is rare in Java because the nested generic types get verbose. The everyday form is a factory method that returns a lambda capturing configuration, such as Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor), Predicate.not(...) or maxLen(20).
